newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch regret post-war "police action" in Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: Dutch regret post-war "police action" in Indonesia.

text.p: The Netherlands has acknowledged that some "police actions" by troops against nationalist Indonesians after World War Two should never have happened, but stopped short of a formal apology.

Dutch soldiers, seeking to regain colonial power till a 1949 settlement, launched several so-called Police Actions on nationalist forces which proclaimed independence in 1945 following Japan's occupation of the Netherlands East Indies.

"Incidents unfortunately took place that should never have happened," junior defence minister Jan Gmelich Meijling told a crowd of 14,000 veterans and their families at an annual memorial service at a monument in the southern Dutch town of Roermond.
"Responsibility for sending troops lay with government and parliament, and nowhere else," he said, adding that the soldiers themselves should not have to take any collective blame.
But Gmelich Meijling, who did not elaborate on the incidents, did not apologise to Indonesia for the violent end to 350 years of Dutch colonial rule there.
The Dutch government's information service published excerpts of his weekend address on Monday.
Some 120,000 Dutch fought in an abortive effort to retake Indonesia between 1945-50 following the Japanese occupation.

During an official visit to Indonesia last year Dutch Queen Beatrix also stopped short of making an official apology, saying: "It deeply saddens us that so many died in that struggle or have had to bear its scars for the rest of their lives."

Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, who did not accompany Beatrix to Indonesia, said at the time: "It is deeply tragic that the transition to actual independence should have caused so much pain, ill-feeling and unbearable suffering."
